lines.text: You know the parts of robot code now: triggers, commands, mechanisms. None of them has anywhere to live yet, so you make the project yourself.
It all starts from one small red icon in the title bar. If you can't find it, you've opened the ordinary editor, not the one the installer gave you.
Pick the template. An example is a finished robot that somebody else wrote, and you're here to write your own.
The second page has a long list, and a couple of entries sound right. Only one matches the code you'll be typing for the rest of the course.
Slow down on the third page. Two of these four fields cause real trouble later if you get them wrong.
The checkbox is the easy one to miss. Without it the program can't run on your laptop, and running it on the laptop is how Workshop 3 drives the real motors.
Then the folder path. Cloud sync rewrites files while the build is using them, and the failure looks like a mistake in your code. School laptops often sync Documents and Desktop without telling you.
The skeleton switches on a second logging tool this course doesn't use. Take those four lines out, or every mechanism gets logged twice and each build prints a note for every field it can't log.
It also ships with nothing for the driver station to pick. You make the teleop file by hand, and keep its name exactly as written, because every lesson after this one opens it.

The command library came with the template. The motor controllers' library didn't. Watch which one you install, because a library with nearly the same name sits right underneath it, and it's the wrong one.
Changing a library kicks off a build by itself. Leave it alone. The first one has a lot to download, so it's slow, and later ones won't be.
If it stops because it couldn't resolve something, that's the network, not you. Reconnect, then run the build again from the same red icon.
You're done when the build ends in success and your file tree matches this list. That's an empty robot that builds, and the next lesson puts the first mechanism in it.
